A modern take on George Orwell's classic novel [i]1984[/i].

The game gives an interesting perspective on topics such as the increasing amount of online surveillance in today's world and how easy it can be to obtain someone's personal data using various social media platforms.

The way certain story events play out and the fate of different characters can change drastically depending on how you handle the tasks given to you. There's also no "game over" state so if you screw up, you'll have to deal with the consequences of your actions.

I'd highly recommend trying this game out. It's a bit dialogue heavy and will require you to browse through a lot of fictional web sites, but you'll definitely enjoy the gripping story it has to offer.

In a time where the internet and smartphones carry all our information, we are all too easy to spy on. What would happen if the government invaded your privacy to fight terrorism? How far would you let them go? Where's the line?

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You does a fantastic job at showing you the dangers of, well, an orwellian society in modern times. All you do in this game is read webpages, eavesdrop conversations, and hack people's devices, and however simple that sounds, it still feels thrilling to upload someone's dirtiest secrests to Big Brother for the government to act upon.

This game integrates gameplay and narrative brilliantly in a way I haven't seen anywhere else. Please do yourself a favor and give this gem a chance.

I finished the game in one straight sitting. It only took about 4 hours and a bit, so no monster feat, but still something I rarely do. It's a complex game with a very deep implied backstory and a very interesting concept. 

One of the few things I didn't like very much was the level of railroading that's mostly kept very elegantly in the background, but sometimes becomes apparent when you overlook a small seemingly insignificant clue that's needed to unlock the next piece of the puzzle. It's not an issue, but it points to the story being "smaller" than it could have been, and that there would have been room for more elaboration and maybe even several intertwining stories. That would of course be a completely diferent game, story-wise, but I can see a possibility for greatness here. 

Don't get me wrong, I LOVED the game and I'll be playing the next one as soon as I have time.

I did a blind playthrough at first, and then went back to do the achievements to see what other fates might have played out. This is the kind of game where you can learn something of your own actions, and even be shocked that good intentions don't always lead to good outcomes.

It's also an episodic game, meaning you can play it in installments, and you can go back and replay previous episodes, though future progress will be erased. Even though I got it free, I think the asking price is fair for its quality and length.

Fun little game. It's heavily text-based - pretty much a visual novel, but with a lot of actual player input, not just clicking "next". The UI is very easy on the eyes, and the game picks out the relevant bits, so it's not like looking for needles in haystacks. I didn't think I'd like it at first, but it really grew on me.

They also did a very good job with the story. It starts a little slow, but they manage to create relatable characters and an engaging plot. I do have a big gripe with it, though - given the nature of the gameplay and the heavy-handed 1984 references, it was clear the intention was to make you feel like one of the bad guys, and make some radical decisions in the end. Well, if that's the case, you might not want to have your "good guys" as manipiulators who kill civilians to get their point across. 

So the twist didn't really do it for me, but that's the beauty of the story - it might get interprreted differently by different people, so I definitely recommend checking it out. Overall - thumbs up.

Game took me 4 hours to complete 1 playthrough, although you can do multiple playthroughs, depending on what information you find and what connections you make. This game is reading intensive, as you will be sifting through web pages, call logs, chat logs, browser histories, etc. There's also quite a bit of filler information, which is to be expected in this kind of job where you are aggregating huge amounts of data and your job is to sift through that information and find the relevant information.

Not every piece of date is true. There are dead ends and outright lies. Your job will be to try to paint an accurate portrait for your agency to do its job correctly. This game does a great job of putting you in the center of the action as you feel as though you are a real investigator. As the story progresses, you become an even bigger part of the action.

This game isn't for everyone. The gameplay mechanic itself can get tedious at varying times. You really don't stray from what you're doing from the start of Chapter 1 all the way to the conclusion in Chapter 5. So if you don't like parsing information, you will be bored. However, the story keeps it all together and gives purpose to your actions. 

[b]Rate 7/10. Really solid game, interesting story, great ending(s), but the gameplay could have used more variety.[/b]

Short version: makes you do Important Choices With Consequences based on very little, very shaky, third hand info. Not fun or challenging or possible to engage with sincerely.

Long version: early in the first ep, during what you might call the tutorial, you are asked to choose between two versions of the truth: that a crime suspect was released and case closed because of A) lack of evidence or B) bribes. You are given no context for this choice other than a news article stating that the official version is A but some people think it might be B. I'm not exaggerating. All you have to go on is the word of a journalist you don't know, reporting the words of other people you don't know regarding an incident you just heard of. Even so the game stresses that anything you report will be taken as The Truth and there will be no possibility to undo the choice.

Orwell is a "profession simulator" style interactive novel where you control a privacy invading government employee, reading peoples emails and watching security cameras.  You're forced to make decisions to progress the story, although in a bit of hamfisted design, the developers obscure a lot of the readily available information you would have just to make the game more "interesting". 

The game is a very dry computer operation simulator where you're stuck using a fake web browser to plod through the tedious game, copying text and clicking on this and that.   I'm sure there's a "watching paint dry" simulator on Steam and it would be just as engaging.  Bonus points for the sheer irony of a game about big brother asking you for your email address so they can spam you and collect data on you.  That kind of dodginess is completely reprehensible, so even if the game was actually any good, I still wouldn't recommend it to make sure the developers are getting the message.
This is a great game that tries to effect you on what kind of person you are (or which ending you want). Truly incredible.
